REGIONAL INDUSTRIAL EXPANSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to express my anger and extreme disappointment at the Government for its complete disregard of the people of Cape Breton. We have waited long enough for some action on the second phase of the business plan for the Sydney Steel Corporation. We are not talking just about economics here, we are talking about the future of an entire area.
The first phase of the business plan was put into effect by the former Liberal Government. Most of that work was completed months ago, long before the deadline runs out this Sunday. It's now almost April and there are still no answers, no plans, and no financial assistance being put forward by the Government and its counterpart in Nova Scotia for the second phase of modernization. How can the Government justify treating people like this? To say it is unfair is a gross understatement.
People are depending on the life of this plant for their existence. It is especially unfair when you consider what the work force has done to make Sydney Steel Corporation a viable operation. The workers have set production records. Liquid steel production increased by 40 per cent in 1984. Rail mill production and total production shipments have increased by 50 per cent. The operating losses for Sydney Steel Corporation have been cut in half, and Sydney Steel will not require any operating grants from the province this year because of an outstanding performance by the work force.
The workers have accomplished this against some incredible odds. There are now just, 1,400 people working, down from 3,000, and 1,000 of those people-

subtopic: EMPLOYMENT
EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on February 6 the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) announced a program called "Challenge '85" in which private industry was to be pivotal in providing 95,000 career oriented wage subsidized jobs for students. On this, the deadline for applications, we have written the Minister in part as follows:
It is now clear that some of our worst fears have materialized. The private sector response you anticipated has not been forthcoming. Many areas of greatest need are not receiving adequate assistance, and the numerous career-related jobs you promised have not occurred. Moreover there appears to be much confusion in the administrative process and a lack of publicity and adequate information almost everywhere.
It is not my intent in writing merely to point out that the program has been a dismal failure, but rather, to offer some constructive advice on how to ensure that as many students as possible will work under the program this summer. In this regard I submit the following:
Eliminate all deadlines for employers and students submitting applications; allow any type of meaningful job-creation program to be considered, including all project applications; and, launch a full scale media campaign to advertise the new changes. Finally, provide Members from all sides of the House with sufficient detail that they may be effectively involved in publicizing the program. Admit ideologically produced failure and get on with the job of creating jobs.

subtopic: FORESTRY
FORESTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise in this House to bring to light an important issue that is of bilateral importance to Canada and the United States. I am speaking of our most precious resource industry, forestry. 1 have just returned from intensive meetings in the United States along with the Minister of State for Forestry (Mr. Merrithew). In our discussions with the U.S. Forestry Service we were able to forge some meaningful lines of communication and co-operation.
Forestry is a resource that transcends boundaries. It is a North American resource, and many of the issues facing the industry, such as insect control, fire fighting, and forestry research, can best be dealt with if both Canada and the U.S. work together. More important, we are working to maintain a secure trading relationship which will be of benefit to both of our nations.
Our Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) really paved the way for such productive relations between our countries. His decision to appoint a Minister of State for Forestry is not only

March 29, 1985
recognized as an important step for the forest industry in Canada but has also received praise around the world. The Quebec summit meeting also contributed to the excellent relationship that now exists between Canada and its greatest friend and trading partner, the United States. This co-operative relationship is going to produce real benefits for Canada's vital forest industry.

TOURISM

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE
UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE
subsubtopic: CALCULATION OF SEVERANCE PAY AS INCOME
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is a sad day for the workers of Canada. As of midnight Sunday, March 31, 1985, vicious changes to the Unemployment Insurance Act will come into effect. These changes will see severance pay and vacation pay being used in the calculation and duration of unemployment insurance benefits. The severance pay change, in particular, is a calculated and cruel blow to those who lose their employment through no fault of their own.
Such workers have traditionally used the severance pay to offset travel expenses in finding alternate work. Now they will be forced to use this lump sum amount to keep body and soul together until they become eligible for unemployment insurance benefits. In such cases it could be up to a period of 20 to 30 weeks, depending on the amount of severance pay.
[DOT] (mo)
Other workers have rolled their severance pay into a registered retirement savings plan in order to prepare for their retirement years. With this change coming about on Sunday, the individual will now be forced to use the money to subsist on a daily basis. This is the ultimate irony from the Government which says it believes in individual self-reliance. This is the last appeal to this Government which claims it will save $60 million by this measure, but is prepared to put $60 million into a bankrupt bank.

subtopic: AGRICULTURE
AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, southeastern Ontario has always been proud of its agricultural industry and the important role it has played in producing food at a reasonable price for consumers not only in Canada but throughout the world. Today in eastern Ontario there is considerable concern in the agricultural community that this sector of the economy is being burdened with an unfair proportion of the cost associated with maintaining food prices affordable by everyone. A recent proposal by the federal Government to implement a cost recovery program for services such as grading, would result in increased costs to the consumer or, worse, to the already hard hit producers.
One such problem which has been brought to my attention is that of the cheese producers in eastern Ontario who, under this proposal, will have to pay for the grading of cheese which is to be exported. As many Members are aware, many cheese factories have closed. Knowing the federal Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) and his concern for the agricultural community, I trust that through consultation and communication a fair and reasonable solution will be found which will be acceptable to the cheese producers and agricultural communities of eastern Ontario.

subtopic: HOUSING
HOUSING

subtopic: IMMIGRATION
IMMIGRATION
subsubtopic: REFUSAL TO ALLOW DETAINEE TO MARRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the right to marry must be defended against interference by immigration officials. Irene McLaughlin, a Canadian citizen, has enjoyed a commonlaw marriage for four years with Hugo Cobos. However, Mr. Cobos has been detained in the immigrant holding centre at the Waldorf-Astoria Hotel in Toronto for six months. Ms. McLaughlin's request to marry him has been denied by Immigration enforcement authorities in Ontario who will neither permit him a day's leave to marry her nor permit them to be married in the Waldorf-Astoria.
Surely Mr. Cobos should be treated no worse than a criminal. Even convicted criminals are allowed to marry in prison. I believe that that right is protected by the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. This is one more reason why, four weeks ago, I asked the Minister to inquire into conditions at the immigrant holding centres. They deny not only the Charter of Rights and Freedoms but also the United Nations minimum standard for prisoners, which Canada has signed.
I am glad the Minister and the Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration have finally undertaken the inquiry into the immigrant holding centres, but meanwhile let Ms. McLaughlin marry Mr. Cobos. I call on the Minister to take immediate action to defend Ms. McLaughlin's right to marry.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of State for Fitness and Amateur Sport. Yesterday in the House the issue of the 1988 Calgary Winter Olympics was raised, but the Minister refused and failed to address his comments to the $200 million commitment which his Government had made to the games.
The Canadian Olympic Organizing Committee and all Canadians are still awaiting those answers. The time for organizing an event of such national magnitude is short. Therefore I ask the Minister when will he inform the House how he will raise the $200 million and what mechanisms will he put in place? We need the assurance to ensure that all Canadians and Olympic participants will have faith in the commitment which has been made by the Government.
Hon. Otto Jelinek (Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur
Sport)): Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to respond to that question. I have been waiting six months for the Hon. Member to stand up and ask one.
I can assure the Hon. Member that the $200-million commitment to Calgary will be kept. As he knows, the Olympic coin program has already been approved by the House and the estimated revenue from that program will be between $40 million and $50 million. As the Hon. Member also knows, the circulating coin program is now before the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates.
As far as my ongoing negotiations with the provinces for the remaining $100 million are concerned, I can assure the Hon. Member that I am comfortable with those negotiations. I have always maintained that an agreement would be signed before the end of this summer. I still believe that the agreement will be signed. In fact there will be a meeting of Ministers on April 19 in Ottawa which will iron out any remaining difficulties. I am confident that an agreement will be signed shortly thereafter.

Mr. Speaker, it is interesting to note that the Minister is complaining about the lack of questions, but when he gets a question he refuses to answer in any different way. We were told in September that an agreement would be made with the provinces. He gave away the lottery without any guarantee. We were told that an agreement would be forthcoming before Christmas, and at Christmas the Minister told us that it would be forthcoming in the
Oral Questions
new year. Now it is March and he says there will be an agreement in the summer. We need a little more sense of action.
How will the Minister raise the $200 million, when the coin program will be lucky if it raises $30 million? How are the provinces going to come in, and when will they come in? Could he give a sense of direction to the Olympic Committee and Canadians in general?

I am confident that we will raise not only the $200 million non-tax revenue dollars for the Olympic Games, but well beyond $200 million.

subtopic: CANADIAN COMMERCIAL BANK FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE ACT
speechtext:
As our House Leader explained yesterday, we voted for the Bill at second reading so that it would go into Committee of the Whole and we would have an opportunity to ask some questions. I must say that I was concerned by the speech made by the Hon. Member for Edmonton South because one would have assumed that, since the Bank was in his constituency, he would have been able to give us some very persuasive reasons for this bail-out. His reasons were weak in the extreme and certainly did not inspire me with confidence. In fact, they reduced my enthusiasm for the Bill. The main thrust of the comments of the Hon. Member for Edmonton South was that this Bank should be rescued because it is a western bank. 1 sincerely hope that the taxpayers of Canada are not going to be asked to contribute this amount of money simply because the Bank is in Alberta and the Minister of Energy was having a difficult time negotiating an agreement with Alberta.
The Hon. Member for Edmonton South attempted to cast the blame for the Bank's difficulties on to the National Energy Program. There was nothing in the National Energy Program that obliged that Bank to invest in a California bank which had a loan portfolio which was distinctly shaky. In view of the speech of the Member for Edmonton South, we must ask more questions about the management of the Canadian Commercial Bank and the quality of the business decisions it took. We must ask if the same management team is still there and a lot of questions about the information that the Government had.

March 29, 1985
Canadian Commercial Bank
When the Minister of State for Finance made her statement in the House on Monday, we were given the impression that the Government received its first information that the Canadian Commercial Bank was in serious difficulty quite recently in the month of March. Later, in response to questioning, the Minister of Finance said that he had received information from the Inspector General in September. Now we learn that even two years ago the American regulatory authorities had been in touch with the Canadian authorities. At that time they were apparently expressing concern about the California bank in and around the time that the Canadian Commercial Bank invested in it.
I would also like to know if the Inspector General of Banks had advised the Canadian Commercial Bank at any time to diversify its holdings. I made a reference in the House a couple of days ago to the statement that is in Part 3 of the Estimates, that it is part of the Inspector General's duty, if he foresees trouble, to encourage a bank to diversify. I would like to know if this obligation was exercised, and when it was exercised.
I would also like an explanation of diversification. As far as I can see from the information we have, the holdings of this Bank were all in the energy field. They may have diversified geographically, but is that to be taken seriously as diversification? Is that what the Inspector General of Banks intended?
I have several other questions, Mr. Chairman, but perhaps I might afford the Minister an opportunity to answer those.

subtopic: CANADIAN COMMERCIAL BANK FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I hope I have kept all the questions straight. If I haven't, 1 know the Hon. Member will ask them again. I would like to start by congratulating you, Mr. Chairman, on your excellent role today in Question Period.
Perhaps I could explain in a little detail the history of the relationship with the California operations. In 1981 the Canadian Commercial Bank acquired a 40 per cent interest in the Westlands Bank. The Westlands Bank was largely involved with real estate loans. The move by the CCB into California was an attempt to diversify geographically. It was involved in the Westlands Bank in the real estate area. At that point real estate markets were very strong. The real estate market in California, as in other areas, later began to decline. The Canadian Commercial Bank, as the major shareholder in the Westlands Bank, increased its participation in the Westlands Bank with an injection of capital to strengthen that operation. The recent problems were through the CCB's agency in California. The agency was involved with oil service and drilling rig loans.
Whether it is a good business decision to diversify geographically within the same industry is obviously a question of where the Board of Directors is heading. Certainly within some kinds of companies one would want to stay in the area where presumably one has expertise. Rather than going into an area where they did not have the expertise, it was better to diversify
geographically and stay with the industry they were familiar with and could bring the best judgment to.
As we know, the Bank was substantially more profitable in the late 1970s. It looked like an aggressive, moving bank. After the real estate market in California began to decline the difficulties were recognized. The oil service industry in California got into difficulty very recently. The Bank has also made other efforts to diversify. It now has branches in Vancouver, Winnipeg, Toronto, Montreal, and Halifax, as well as in western Canada. I think the correct business decisions were taken with regard to diversification. They perhaps did not work quickly enough, but I think the Bank made some appropriate moves on diversification.

subtopic: CANADIAN COMMERCIAL BANK FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE ACT
speechtext: Could the Minister also give us the history of the involvement of the Inspector General of Banks? There is a newspaper report that the Inspector General's office has been receiving a steady stream of inquiries from the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, the U.S. equivalent of the Canadian Deposit Insurance Corporation, from the U.S. Federal Reserve Board, and from the California banking superintendent's office over a two-year period. If this is the case, could we know what action was taken over that two-year period?

subtopic: CANADIAN COMMERCIAL BANK FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE ACT
speechtext: Since there were overlapping jurisdictions, there was a connection made early in 1983, I believe. An official of the Inspector General's office went to California to look at the Westlands acquisition. There was not, as was implied in the newspaper, a steady stream of phone calls and telexes. There was simply, on an occasional basis, as would be normal, conversations between the two regulatory bodies. They were actually quite rare. There was evidence that the West-lands Bank was improving. As I understand it, both regulatory agencies were satisfied that, while the problems were obviously severe, they were not critical.

subtopic: CANADIAN COMMERCIAL BANK FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I trust that we will be hearing questions from a variety of Members today as we go through this Bill.
I would like to return to the point that my colleague from Trinity was referring to a moment ago. On January 25, 1983 the Governor of the Bank of Canada was obviously concerned enough about the situation to phone the national newspaper. The Globe and Mail. He convinced The Globe and Mail, at least, that everything was fine, that the Commercial Bank was profitable, solvent and there were no problems. Will the Minister explain if that was an accurate statement at that time when the Governor of the Bank was saying that it was solvent and profitable? Did he actually have evidence at that point on which to make that statement or was he simply trying to calm down investors in Canada as well as elsewhere?
March 29, 1985

subtopic: CANADIAN COMMERCIAL BANK FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE ACT
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I think that statement was made by the Governor after consultation with the Inspector General. It was made in relation to the resignation of Mr. Eaton as the Chief Executive Officer of the Bank. Over the two or three months prior to that, there had been some building up of concern around Mr. Eaton's relationship with Mr. Rosenberg. Throughout that time, as the concern and the pressure on the trust company situation arose, I think the Governor took responsible action by indicating that this Bank was not connected with that scandalous affair because of action taken through the resignation of Howard Eaton.

subtopic: CANADIAN COMMERCIAL BANK FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have a general question for the Minister. My office, and I suspect many other offices, has received many phone calls and telegrams from people who are very concerned about what kind of signal is being sent by the Government. According to this Bill, the Government is spending at least $75 million; $60 million of that is coming from the federal Government directly, to bail out this failing bank and ensure that it will not fail.
Does this mean that from this point on it may be well recognized that any bank that gets into financial difficulty will have the full support of the federal Government, that it will be guaranteed that the federal Government will bail out any failing bank or financial institution in the country?

subtopic: CANADIAN COMMERCIAL BANK FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this situation was caused by an isolated incident. There are no other financial institutions in the country at the moment that are appearing to be insolvent in any way. I would like to make it clear that other institutions are not being looked at under the circumstances that we are talking about now. I want that absolutely clear for the House, the people of Canada and the depositors in our financial institutions.
If any organization under my legislative or regulatory jurisdiction was to come to me with difficulties, I would look at each situation as it stood. I can make no commitment at this time either for or against what happens in the very unlikely event that we are faced with this again.

subtopic: CANADIAN COMMERCIAL BANK FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE ACT
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, why is there an interest-free loan? I realize that we are asking the taxpayers of Canada to provide $60 million-a loan, in a sense-to this troubled bank to assist it to get back on its feet. I think we support that notion but when other people obtain money from the federal Government in one way or another, they usually pay interest. Why would we not charge a bank interest as well?

subtopic: CANADIAN COMMERCIAL BANK FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the support package was designed so that the participants would be repaid the principal amount interest-free, except that in addition there would be warrants to purchase equity in the Bank issued on a pro rata basis to the support group, which could be exercised for ten years after the principal is paid back, so that there is a return
Canadian Commercial Bank
to the taxpayers and to the support package participants in general. The warrants can be exercised at a very modest price and the warrants, as the Bank is profitable, will have a trading value and be able to be sold. That will be a return to the participants in the support package, including the taxpayers.

subtopic: CANADIAN COMMERCIAL BANK FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE ACT
speechtext: The Minister says that we will be able to purchase these warrants at a very modest price. Since it is a failing bank and because its shares have virtually collapsed on the stock exchange, is it any surprise that we are able to obtain these warrants at a very reasonable and modest cost? Assuming that the Bank will eventually get back on its feet, we will in fact receive a fair return for an equity position, in a sense.

subtopic: CANADIAN COMMERCIAL BANK FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE ACT
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I find the Hon. Member's vocabulary somewhat hysterical. This is not a failing bank.

subtopic: CANADIAN COMMERCIAL BANK FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE ACT
speechtext: It has already failed.

subtopic: CANADIAN COMMERCIAL BANK FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE ACT
speechtext: The Bank is not failing. It is not failing because it has had a very strong support package from the private sector, from the province and from the Government of Canada. This Bank is a solvent bank.

subtopic: CANADIAN COMMERCIAL BANK FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the point I want to make to the Minister is that we are in the House today at Committee of the Whole stage of a Bill that is meant to bail out a bank. Regardless of the title, we are bailing out the Canadian Commercial Bank. The reason we are doing this is that it had failed. Its stocks had crashed on the stock market. People were very concerned about its future. It is perfectly clear that if this bail-out package had not been assembled, that bank would not be in existence. I realize that by doing this we will rescue what had been a failed bank. It is not going to be failed after this package is stickhandled through its various jurisdictions.
Why is this Bill necessary if this bank was, in the past, in a healthy, solvent situation? Why is this bail-out situation to the tune of almost a quarter billion dollars-$225 million-necessary if the bank was in good health?

subtopic: CANADIAN COMMERCIAL BANK FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE ACT
speechtext: I am trying to indicate to the Canadian public in a responsible way, unlike the Hon. Member, that we came to Canadians and to the House and presented a problem which had arisen, together with a solution to that problem. If he wants to make irresponsible statements about failing institutions, they can all come crashing down around our heads. The point is that there was a problem and a resolution of that problem. Therefore the Bank is not failing. Could we please make that very clear?

subtopic: CANADIAN COMMERCIAL BANK FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE ACT
speechtext: It had failed.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: CANADIAN COMMERCIAL BANK FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, let me return to the reasons for the failure of the Bank. Following some strong advice from the Inspector General of Banks, Canadian Commercial Bank was told to diversify in 1981, I believe. It diversified with the

March 29, 1985
Canadian Commercial Bank
purchase of Westlands in the United States. They also opened offices in Montreal, Toronto and Halifax.

subtopic: CANADIAN COMMERCIAL BANK FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE ACT
speechtext: If the Bank moved out of Canada to go to California to finance oil rigs, which is different from the answer given a moment ago to my colleague-the Minister said the Bank was going into real estate,-if the oil rigs were going at a tenth of their value in California and this Canadian Commercial Bank was indeed trying to diversify, why did it go into the oil business in California? speechtext:

The Westlands Bank went through some difficulties with its real estate. There appears, as I understand it, more stability. The Westlands Bank was also involved with computer software. There was an effort to diversify in other areas, and it went through a difficult period. The softwave end is now consolidated into the Canadian Commercial Bank, is a profitable operation and over time will be contributing to the consolidated earnings of the Bank.
The agency, on the other hand, was involved with these oil rig loans. Those have become a problem really very recently. I want to read from something that appeared in The New York Times describing what had happened in a similar market in Texas. I shall give the Hon. Member the clipping and it will provide an idea of what has happened over the last three months and why this appeared to come out of nowhere. This
article is headed "Oil Industry's bad cold. Starts to give explorers, drillers, shippers, and banks pneumonia. Exploration and production are the heart of the industry. But the pulse is weakening". In another area of the article it says: "2,175 drilling rigs are operating in U.S., down 612 from December", and I think it is "299 from last February".

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: CANADIAN COMMERCIAL BANK FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE ACT

I appreciate the answer, Mr. Chairman. It was given in an informative manner and 1 thank the Minister for that. I thought the OPEC price breakdown, the international market being what it was, had had a direct effect on oil exploration in California and I do think there is merit to that argument.

subtopic: CANADIAN COMMERCIAL BANK FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE ACT
speechtext: The dilution of the existing equity will be about 75 per cent. In terms of what will be the value, it will depend upon the Bank's future profitability and how that is regarded by people who are buying and selling the stock. I could not give him an answer on that.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: CANADIAN COMMERCIAL BANK FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE ACT
speechtext: In view of the fact that the Minister said there would be a dilution of 75 per cent of the existing shares, what steps will the Government take to prevent this dilution from harming the investment in employee pension funds, representing thousands of employees in all parts of the country? What will the Government do to prevent damage to these funds or some possible risk to the base which these pension funds are supposed to represent?

subtopic: CANADIAN COMMERCIAL BANK FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE ACT
speechtext: Most of the pension funds represented among the shareholders are defined benefit plans whereby they are both employee and employer contributions. However, as the Hon. Member knows, as defined benefit plans the employer is obligated to ensure that the defined benefits are paid at the time of retirement. There will be no negative impact on the payment to either current retirees or future retirees.

subtopic: CANADIAN COMMERCIAL BANK FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, understandably the Minister objected to the use of the world "failing" in terms of the Bank. Indeed, the Bank is now in very good shape, having had a large infusion of new moneys.
I want to question the use of taxpayers' money in this bail-out. Regional banks in Canada have not had a conspicuous record of success but in the past, when it has been necessary to rescue a regional bank, it has been done by the banking authorities. Indeed Canada's banks have a most enviable reputation. In this country we do not have banks fail, of which we can all be very proud. In the past the banks themselves have acted and used their own money to ensure that their good reputation was maintained.
In this case we have the banks contributing but we also have large requirements for tax dollars. Would the Minister care to comment on the reports which are being carried in the newspapers that we are in this situation because the Government of Alberta wanted control to remain in Alberta and would not allow "eastern banks" to rescue them?

March 29, 1985
Canadian Commercial Bank

subtopic: CANADIAN COMMERCIAL BANK FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think that was a somewhat misleading report. There have been mergers in the past. We looked at a number of possibilities and we came up with what we felt was the most attractive solution for everyone. If a bank gets into trouble and gets merged into one of the big five banks, we could end up with no regional banks. I am not sure that is where we want to go. I think we would like to have some regional banks as long as they are viable. Maybe that requires our help. It required the help of the province. The province indicated its commitment. We indicated that we felt it was responsible for the Government to be involved. It is in all our interests.
In connection with some of the things that have been going on in the States, simply the rumour of potential trouble in the Texas banking system triggered a move in the U.S. dollar. It is not only in the interests of Toronto or Calgary, it is in our interest to indicate to Canadians and to the world that we have faith in the system and in this Bank. We want to ensure that there is a place in Canada for regional banks, provided they are viable, solvent and contributing to local businesses in an economic way.

subtopic: CANADIAN COMMERCIAL BANK FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE ACT
speechtext:
We all fully support the position that confidence is important and that it is important to move quickly. However, I have not had a clear answer to my question as to why taxpayers' dollars have to be used or the one as to why the banks, as they have done in the past, did not assume responsibility for protecting their very excellent reputation.
The total assets of this particular bank are less than 1 per cent of the assets of big banks. Is the Minister saying that the policy of the Government is that small regional banks are so important ideologically or philosophically that we put taxpayers' money into them rather than ask the banks to come to their aid when they are very well able to do so without taking taxpayers' money?

subtopic: CANADIAN COMMERCIAL BANK FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE ACT
speechtext: 1 think the banks did come to the aid of this bank. After all, as a group they are putting in $60 million and through the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation, which is funded by financial institutions, there is another $75 million. I think they have indicated very strong support for the Bank and are committed to helping to support the system. There is a partnership which I believe is perfectly valid in, first, indicating confidence in the system and, second, in looking at a regional institution.

subtopic: CANADIAN COMMERCIAL BANK FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE ACT
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I seek two or three points of clarification from the Hon. Minister. In the letter the Minister wrote to my Leader, a copy of which was sent to my House Leader, she said that the undertaking by respective Governments to purchase the subordinated debt of the CCB would cost the Canadian Government $13 million. Could she elaborate on that? I do not understand to what that particular paragraph refers.

subtopic: CANADIAN COMMERCIAL BANK FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, there is within the capital structure or framework of this Bank subordinated debentures.
The subordinated debentures carry interest. The three levels of Government have purchased those debentures and they will be repaid. We then become creditors of the Bank at that level, in addition to the $60 million.

subtopic: CANADIAN COMMERCIAL BANK FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE ACT
speechtext: The Minister knows that the last clause in the Bill refers to $75 million to be paid out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund. We in the House consistently refer to the $60 million which it will cost Canadian taxpayers, yet the Bill indicates $75 million. Could the Minister explain the difference between those two figures?

subtopic: CANADIAN COMMERCIAL BANK FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE ACT
speechtext: The amount referred to includes the $60 million in the support package and the $13 million worth of debentures.

subtopic: CANADIAN COMMERCIAL BANK FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE ACT
speechtext:
I have another couple of questions, and then I will turn the floor over to some of my colleagues.
With regard to this whole business of a bank that in the past got itself into some financial difficulty and is now going to be okay, this is certainly a reflection on the Board of Directors and the management of the Bank to a certain extent, perhaps to a large extent. Since we are asking in this Bill for the taxpayers of Canada to come up with $75 million to assist this Bank and presumably launch it in a new and successful direction, can the Minister explain what has happened to the people who were responsible for causing the situation and in fact approved imprudent loans and approved a financial program that resulted in the Bank getting into severe financial difficulty? What has happened to the senior management? What has happened to the Board of Directors? Does the Minister have any observations on reports that a number of senior officials of the Bank sold stocks of the Bank prior to this particular item becoming public information, presumably at least saving their own necks in terms of stocks they held?

subtopic: CANADIAN COMMERCIAL BANK FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in terms of the management of the Bank, as far as I and my officials are aware, and my judgment at this stage, the chief executive officer acted very responsibly in coming to us when he did with the difficulty. The attempts at diversification across Canada and into California were essentially responsible moves. The board has acted in a responsible way, as has management. We would indeed seek representation on the Board of Directors of the Bank. The Inspector General will have two people monitoring the problem loans. We would hope to add to the Board of Directors. If indeed we find it to be different than our impression is now, we will take the appropriate action.
There have been a number of changes in the management since the departure of Howard Eaton and there have been moves to strengthen both the board and management since that time. Unfortunately, the stronger management and the stronger board came at a time when the situation was becoming more difficult. Our understanding is that they have acted responsibly.
March 29, 1985

I am obviously most disappointed to find out today that one executive of the Bank did indeed sell his preferred shares. There was no indication to the management of the Bank at that stage of the extent of the difficulty. It would have been clear to anyone who read the annual report that the deferred dividend was not in fact covered by earnings. 1 am extraordinarily disappointed to see that and we will be looking into it.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: CANADIAN COMMERCIAL BANK FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE ACT
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the Minister said that the amount to be appropriated under this Bill is to cover the $60 million as part of the main rescue package and $13 million to purchase subordinated debentures. That comes to $73 million and the amount requested in the Bill is $75 million. Can she tell us what the other $2 million will be used for?

subtopic: CANADIAN COMMERCIAL BANK FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE ACT
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, what will be spent will be no more than is necessary. There is the possibility of some accrued interest that would have to be covered on debentures over and above the $13 million.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: CANADIAN COMMERCIAL BANK FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE ACT
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, 1 wish to turn briefly to another matter. With respect to the loans in the oil sector in California that went bad, can the Minister tell me when they were made? In particular, how many were made after the visit by the Inspector General of Banks to the Minister on September 14?

subtopic: CANADIAN COMMERCIAL BANK FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE ACT
speechtext: I am not quite clear, Mr. Chairman. There was no visit on September 14. Is the Hon. Member referring to the letter from the Inspector General of September 24 last? The letter was as a result of the Inspector General's annual review which he undertakes for all banks under his jurisdiction. Probably many of the oil service loans would be rolled over. They would be financing rigs once the industry started to face some difficulties. As the oil business declined, that is when it would have shown up.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: CANADIAN COMMERCIAL BANK FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am asking these questions to try and determine-and I would have hoped the Minister would have had this breakdown-how many of these problem loans were already on the books in a way that they should have been brought to the attention of or discovered by the Inspector General of Banks and his staff, and how many were made after September for the first time.
With respect to the latter category of loans, I would like to know what changes, if any, had been made in the executive officers of the Bank who were in place from September to March 14 as well as in the board of directors which was in place from September to March 14. If no changes have been made, what changes are contemplated?

subtopic: CANADIAN COMMERCIAL BANK FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I believe that the Board of Directors is the same now as it was on September 24. September 24 was a letter from the Inspector General to the Minister indicating that the Bank was facing some difficulties. The situation at that time, if I remember, going through the annual report and the quarterly financial statements, was that the Bank was profitable in the first and third quarters of its last
Canadian Commercial Bank
fiscal year which ended March 31. Somehow it is written in stone that that is when the bank year ends. In the second and fourth quarters, it was not profitable. It was marginally profitable in the first quarter of the current fiscal year. Therefore, it has been dealing with an unstable situation.
There was no evidence that the board or the management was acting in an inappropriate way. Along with its efforts to expand their business base, either geographically or into other industries, there was also a retrenching within the energy sector. I think these were normal business decisions, faced with a difficult situation.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: CANADIAN COMMERCIAL BANK FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I want to come back to try and understand this question of warrants. There is a participation agreement that will be drafted. There are participation certificates that are going to be issued. I take it that this is synonymous with the warrants we are talking about. In the memorandum of intent, we read at page 5:
The rights or warrants shall expire ten years after the day that CCB has paid to the Support Group an amount of money equal to the full amount paid by the Support Group for their Participation Certificates.
The sentence following surprises me:
It is recognized that the rights provided for in this paragraph may not be granted under present legislation.
Can the Minister explain that to me?

subtopic: CANADIAN COMMERCIAL BANK FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE ACT
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I should have the agreement here somewhere, I apologize. This was a degree of protection asked for by the banks. Our lawyers have satisfied us, and we have been dealing not only with Department of Finance lawyers but with Tory and Tory in Toronto-

subtopic: CANADIAN COMMERCIAL BANK FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE ACT
speechtext: That's understandable.

subtopic: CANADIAN COMMERCIAL BANK FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE ACT
speechtext: -who assure us that this is legal at the moment. We are assured on that point. As this was being drawn up, this was essentially a comfort clause for the participants.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: CANADIAN COMMERCIAL BANK FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE ACT
speechtext: The Minister was asked a few minutes ago by my colleague from Windsor West if she had the list of loans and depositors. In that same agreement, it states that the schedule of assets will be printed soon. I wonder if she could tell us what the schedule of assets is and when can we expect the schedule to be made public?

subtopic: CANADIAN COMMERCIAL BANK FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the schedule refers to the problem loans. It involves clients of the Bank and there are certain sensitivities in making that list available. 1 am prepared to discuss it, but I would have some difficulty in making it public. Certainly I could provide a breakdown of the numbers of the loans in particular categories. I have some of that in broad strokes at the moment, but I do not have a complete and individual list. The support group will be participating in that schedule of assets.

March 29, 1985
Canadian Commercial Bank

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: CANADIAN COMMERCIAL BANK FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE ACT
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the Minister has suggested that giving the full details of the problem loans-the amounts, the names of the borrowers and so on-may create a problem. I presume she is referring to the secrecy provisions of the Bank Act. I would like to know whether any of that information would otherwise be available under U.S. law-the U.S. securities law, the U.S. banking law or the access to information law. If that is the case, I trust that the Minister will not hide behind our law in not disclosing that information.

subtopic: CANADIAN COMMERCIAL BANK FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE ACT
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I would be happy to explore that. Our understanding is that in both countries common law protects the public under those circumstances. Indeed, if there is a difficulty with that we will have further discussions on it.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: CANADIAN COMMERCIAL BANK FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE ACT
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I would like to return to the matter of problem loans. There is something about the whole aspect of problem loans in the United States oil sector which I find puzzling. The Government has said over and over again that the national energy policy created difficulties for the oil and gas sector in Canada. Yet the loans which got the company into difficulty were loans that were made to the oil sector in the United States. As far as I know, the United States does not have a national energy policy. In fact, when the Government was in opposition it always pointed to the American policy on energy as a model which we should follow. Can she explain how it was that the loans which tipped the balance and precipitated this very unusual bail-out situation were in the oil sector of the United States?

subtopic: CANADIAN COMMERCIAL BANK FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, with respect to the financial institutions within Canada, if we look at any economic statistics we will see that western Canada has faced a considerable amount of difficulty over the last three or four years. That difficulty resulted in part because investment capital left the country as the energy business declined. As well, some Canadian capital left. That situation was not unique to western Canada, but it was certainly endemic there, and some of the later prosperity in the oil industry in the United States was not shared in western Canada.
I do not think I have ever stated that the fact oil prices are now declining, and drilling activity in California is on the decline, had anything to do with the national energy policy. The point is, there was a period when the industry was profitable and the United States was benefiting but our industry was not.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: CANADIAN COMMERCIAL BANK FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the Minister has made my point, which is that there can be problems in the oil sector quite apart from the national energy policy. That was proven by what happened in the United States. The argument of her Party is that outside Government and inside Government there is some type of ongoing nirvana in the energy sector in the United States because it did not and does not have a national energy program. Yet the loans which got this Bank into trouble were loans made to the oil sector in the United States.
In the Minister's press release of March 25, she indicated that if those loans had been made to the oil sector in a country where there was no equivalent national energy policy and had not gone bad, we would be doing something else today. The French version of her press release of March 25 reads as follows:

The support program is designed to provide the Canadian Commercial Bank with enough funds to maintain its solvency, following a recent and serious deterioration in its loan portfolio in the United States.

It was explained that this was particularly in reference to loans in the oil sector in the United States. I want to put on the record that the type of energy policy which is followed by the United States has certainly not prevented a decline in that sector which led to the loans made by the Canadian Commercial Bank going bad, and that in large part precipitated this bail-out situation.

subtopic: CANADIAN COMMERCIAL BANK FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE ACT
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, if the energy industry in Canada had participated in that more profitable time in the early 1980s after the national energy policy, which triggered an earlier decline in the oil industry in Canada than in the United States, then perhaps the Bank would have been stronger and have had the resources to absorb its other losses. I do not particularly want to carry on this argument all afternoon, but I would be happy to do so if the Hon. Member wants to pursue it.

subtopic: CANADIAN COMMERCIAL BANK FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have just begun to focus on this particular question. Frankly, I am appalled at what the Government of Canada is doing in terms of rushing in to rescue this particular private enterprise, particularly in view of the many statements which were made by members of the Conservative Party before they assumed government. When Conservative Members were in opposition, they criticized the bail-out of losers in other sectors, particularly in the industrial sector. I am also appalled at the double standard which is being applied here.
Perhaps I could begin by asking the Minister whether any similar type of terms, in terms of a rescue, will be made available to any western Canadian companies which were put into bankruptcy by the action of the Canadian Commercial Bank in the last two or three years by calling in its loans.

subtopic: CANADIAN COMMERCIAL BANK FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have tried to explain to the House that this solution was arrived at because, in the judgment of knowledgeable people-including the Governor of the Bank of Canada, a group of six chartered banks, the Inspector General and the Province of Alberta-the Bank would have been a viable operation if the capital was provided to resolve its loans problems. I have looked at the situation and I believe we came up with a solution which was in the interests of the small business community of western Canada. If we had liquidated the Bank, those people would be in enormous difficulty today. I believe we looked at the operation in a fairly
March 29, 1985

hard-headed way and decided that it was in the interests of all to participate, along with the banks and the two provinces.

subtopic: CANADIAN COMMERCIAL BANK FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have to say that hard-headed looks awfully soft-headed to me. I am sure that any small business which faced bankruptcy or had its loans called could have been rescued if a deal such as this had been brought in and money was offered which was equivalent to twice the equity which was shown by that particular entity a few months before.
I would like to put on the record that the equity for the Canadian Commercial Bank, which it showed in its 1984 annual report, was in the order of $110 million, or $115 million in terms of capital and attained surplus. So the money which is being brought in, which is tantamount to equity because of the terms of repayment-which are on a never-never basis-is equal to more than double the equity of the Bank. Sure, we can rescue it on that basis but that does not suggest to me that it is a particularly good deal.
I return to my question: What arrangements are being made in order to provide similar terms to any western Canadian small business which was forced to go into receivership, bankruptcy or forced to close by having its loans called by the Canadian Commercial Bank?

subtopic: CANADIAN COMMERCIAL BANK FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we have undertaken to look after the borrowers and the depositors of this Bank. The Bank is keeping them on its books because they are viable operations. If business decisions have been taken around other institutions, I have not made them, and in the judgment of the people who are lending the money to the public, these decisions are viable.
What the Hon. Member is assuming is that the Bank should have kept on its books all of the bad loans, in which case it would be even worse off today.

subtopic: CANADIAN COMMERCIAL BANK FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE ACT
speechtext: I am suggesting there is a double standard. The Minister acknowledges that there was no assistance provided by the Government of Canada, by the other chartered banks or by the Governments of Alberta and British Columbia in the case of borrowers from the Canadian Commercial Bank who, for various reasons, were forced into bankruptcy, had to cease business or had their loans called by this particular bank over the last two or three years. It's a double standard when a bank get rescued and its customers do not. It's a double standard where if you are big enough the current Government of Canada is prepared to bail you out, but if you are a little guy or gal, you are not going to get bailed out. Will the Minister not acknowledge that there is a double standard there?

subtopic: CANADIAN COMMERCIAL BANK FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE ACT
speechtext: I will not acknowledge that there is a double standard.

subtopic: CANADIAN COMMERCIAL BANK FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE ACT
speechtext:
Then the Minister is wrong in failing to acknowledge that, Mr. Chairman.
Canadian Commercial Bank
I would like to go into the terms of this financial assistance and then ask the Minister if she can give us in present value terms-her officials can begin to work on this now-what the Government of Canada and the CDIC portion of the rescue package is going to be. She has acknowledged that the takeover of the subordinated debentures is going to cost the Government $13 million. Since that is at the very end of the queue in terms of any potential repayment or commencement of interest payments, that is $13 million which is a net cost to the people of Canada and which effectively we will never get back.
According to the Memorandum of Intent which was given to my Leader yesterday, the money which has been given to the Bank is not generally for support of all of its obligations. It is specifically related to $544 million of problem loans which have an estimated realizeable value of $289 million. The difference between those two figures is $255 million. That is the money which is being advanced by the support group, including the CDIC and the Government of Canada.
It is my understanding that at least a substantial portion of those problem loans are in fact in the United States. What the devil a regional bank is doing in California, when it's based in Alberta, is beyond me. The terms of payments are: heads, the bank wins, and tails, the Government of Canada and the other support group members lose. Specifically, if any payments on any loan in the portfolio are made, those payments will be applied not to the Government of Canada but to the CCB. I am told the written down portion has in fact been paid up. This is in the agreement. In other words, if there is a $5 million loan which has been written down to $2.5 million, and the borrower repays $1 million, the Government of Canada does not get a nickel back. That entire $1 million goes to the CCB, and the next $1 million goes to the CCB.
I would record for Hansard, Mr. Chairman, that the Minister is looking extremely puzzled as though she does not realize that the Bank wins-

subtopic: CANADIAN COMMERCIAL BANK FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE ACT
speechtext: I am concentrating on what you are saying. Don't say things like that. Retract it, please.

subtopic: CANADIAN COMMERCIAL BANK FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE ACT
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the Minister states that she is concentrating. I say that she looks puzzled to hear exactly what this means spelled out in terms that ordinary people can in fact understand. That is what I think we have to look at. While my Party has agreed that we will facilitate the passage of this Bill, I want to say that as one Member of Parliament I think it is an appallingly bad deal for the people of Canada. I think it is an appallingly bad message to give to all of those farmers, mortgage holders and other people who have had their lives destroyed by the banks over the course of the last few years.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: CANADIAN COMMERCIAL BANK FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE ACT
speechtext: Speak up, we can't hear you.

subtopic: CANADIAN COMMERCIAL BANK FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE ACT
speechtext:
The banks have made huge profits on the backs of Canadians and now what happens is that we come along and spend $60 million or $73 million-goodness knows how much money-in order to bail out one particular bank.

March 29, 1985
Canadian Commercial Bank
No heads are being made to roll. That particular bank executive who profiteered by selling his preferred shares when he could see that the handwriting was on the wall for the Bank is not being forced to resign. The Minister has no sense of anger at what was being done. Whether or not the ultimate decision was made to rescue the Bank, it would be at least good to see some anger coming from the other side, Mr. Chairman, to indicate that the Government of Canada does not like the people of Canada to be held up to ransom the way this is occurring in this particular case.

subtopic: CANADIAN COMMERCIAL BANK FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I can shout just as loudly as the Hon. Member.
I am trying to carry on a reasonable and rational discussion around what we are trying to do. I am trying to be as open as I possibly can with Hon. Members of this House. I do not appreciate the tone taken by the Hon. Member opposite who has decided to use his anger for dramatic purposes. 1 am attempting to do something for the people of this country and I do not hear a whole lot of support coming from the Hon. Member personally around the kinds of things we are attempting to do for the small borrower in Alberta. I would like to bring this discussion to a close and get on with providing information.

subtopic: CANADIAN COMMERCIAL BANK FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I want to say to the Minister in a calm way that I have been dealing for the last couple of days with the case of a small business person who has a contract with a Crown Corporation-which I will not mention-of the Government of Canada. That Crown Corporation has determined to drive that small business person out of business. He may in fact have to go into receivership. I hope not. My efforts to intervene and try to get the Crown Corporation to at least extend the contract in a reasonable way have failed. The Crown Corporation states by way of a reason that it is under pressure to do better and not to contribute to the deficit. So one small business person, with five or six jobs depending on his particular business, is being put to the wall and in fact will probably close effective this afternoon.
If I am angry, Mr. Chairman, it is because there seems to be such a difference in the treatment of the rich and powerful in this country compared to the little guy and gal. I speak of that because I happened to have spent two or three hours this week on that particular case. I know the Minister has worked long and hard and I appreciate her sincerity with respect to her efforts to rescue this particular corporation. However, when I mention the double standard, I am saying that certainly the Government of Canada did not intervene on behalf of a lot of small business people in the Province of Alberta who faced, as we all know, very difficult times. It has been really tough over the last two or three years. But the Government of Canada has not intervened.
All of the banks, including the private banks which are part of the support group, have in fact forced people to the wall and beyond. As the Minister well knows from her contact with western Canada, mortgage holders and home owners have had to walk away from their homes and drop the keys into the mail
slot of the nearest bank because they could not afford to continue. That kind of treatment has not provoked the Government of Canada-either the old one or the new-to act. When interest rates were up around 18 per cent or 19 per cent, the Government showed no mercy. But now mercy is shown in the case of this particular bank which, to put it mildly, has made a series of extremely unwise investments, particularly the extension of its regional mandate to go down into California.
I appreciate that the Minister wants to have some constructive comments. I will seek to make them. But it is difficult to do so in light of the agreement which has been entered into. As I stated before, any payments on any loan in the problem portfolio will first go to the CCB. Then any additional amounts to be paid will go to Canada, Alberta and the bank group in proportion to their participation. The CDIC is at the end of the queue.
In view of the fact that these are problem loans and any money which accrues as a result of those loans to the three prime members of the support group would accrue only if the loans returned more than the currently written-down value, I think I would be fair in suggesting to the Minister that the chances of repayment to the Government of Canada under Clause 3(a) would be limited and probably negligible. Is that fair?

subtopic: CANADIAN COMMERCIAL BANK FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE ACT
speechtext: Our loans are repaid out of the profits of the Bank on the good loans, so that we are getting a participation from their good loans by getting 50 per cent of their pre-tax earnings. We tried to negotiate the deal in such a way that the Bank would have the capital to get on with its responsibilities as a bank, that we would take 50 per cent of earnings and share the proceeds on the problem loans.

subtopic: CANADIAN COMMERCIAL BANK FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE ACT
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I would point out to the Minister that the Bank's pre-tax earnings back in 1984 amounted to $804,000. If the Government of Canada and the other members of the support group were to be repaid out of those pre-tax earnings, it would take approximately 62.5 years before the people of Canada were repaid. I recognize that a good portion of the problem loans may yield some revenues, but all we are doing with the $250 million is basically subsidizing the Bank for those portions of the problem loans which it does not now expect to be repaid. Therefore, the $225 million package cannot be expected to contribute appreciably to the pre-tax earnings of the Canadian Commercial Bank; is that correct?

subtopic: CANADIAN COMMERCIAL BANK FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE ACT
speechtext:
The profitability of the Bank will depend on a number of things, First, I think there will be a better recovery within the Bank's markets. Secondly, it has its bad loans off the books. Thirdly, it has an injection of $250 million in cash on which it will earn a return, so that will contribute to its profits. So we would expect the Bank's profitability to improve quite materially.
March 29, 1985

subtopic: CANADIAN COMMERCIAL BANK FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE ACT
speechtext:
I am not quite sure if I understand that because the Bank is going to have to record in its statements a write-down of approximately $255 million. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if I may I would like to thank Hon. Members for accommodating me. I understood earlier in the day that because of the pressure of House business it was going to be very difficult for me to make a statement and presumably receive a few questions afterwards.
If I may, this statement that I am making is really on my own behalf and on behalf of the Minister for International Trade (Mr. Kelleher) who is in Sault Ste. Marie today.
There have been, as we know, a number of so-called voluntary export restraint understandings with respect to Japanese automobile exports to Canada in the last four years. These understandings are often referred to as VERs. The current arrangement is scheduled to expire March 31, 1985. These VERs have been intended to provide an orderly development of Japanese exports while the Canadian automotive industry was undertaking substantial efforts to restructure and modernize its operations, and to preserve the large number of jobs in this sector. Canada has not imposed import quotas on Japanese passenger cars. They have been administered by the Japanese Government in co-operation with the Japanese Automobile Manufacturers Association.
In recent weeks ministerial discussions have taken place with the various private sector groups directly concerned with the question of Japanese motor vehicle exports to Canada, including representatives of the Motor Vehicle Manufacturers Association, the Automotive Parts Manufacturers Association, the United Auto Workers, the Japanese Automobile Manufacturers Association and the Canadian Association of Japanese Automobile Dealers.
These consultations allowed us to consider the implications for Canada of the rapid changes in the international competitive environment, including the United States of America's decision to allow its restraint understanding with Japan to lapse at the end of March, 1985; the very low level of Japanese automotive investment in Canada; the tendency of the Japanese vehicle manufacturers to concentrate their North American investments in the U.S.A., as well as the emergence of new suppliers of passenger cars to Canada. The impact upon Canadian consumers of restrained access to Japanese passenger cars was also reviewed.
Taking these consultations into account, the Government has reviewed its policy and is now affirming its commitment to a strong and internationally competitive Canadian automotive industry. It also recognizes that the automobile industry is crucial to the growth of the Canadian economy and provides
Automobile Quotas
an essential market for many other industries throughout the country.
Given the expiry on March 31 of the current voluntary restraint understanding on Japanese automobile exports to Canada, senior Canadian officials met recently with Japanese authorities to emphasize the differences between the U.S.A. and the Canadian situation, as well as to explore possible ways and means of avoiding the disruption of the Canadian market.
In addition, the Minister for International Trade has written to the Japanese Minister of International Trade and Industry to bring to his attention the very low level of participation by Japanese motor vehicle producers in the Canadian automotive industry. The letter also stressed the need to maintain a stable market environment in Canada after April 1.
The Government anticipates a response from the Japanese Government in the near future. While the Government fully expects that the Japanese share of the Canadian automotive market will not increase during the forthcoming period of consultations, it will monitor the situation closely to ensure that the Canadian market is not disrupted and that Canadian jobs are not put at risk. The Government intends to give high priority to this important issue and will continue discussions with Japanese authorities with a view to developing a longer term, mutually beneficial automotive relationship.

Mr. Speaker, I must begin by expressing disappointment in the Minister's statement, not only on behalf of the Official Opposition, but on behalf of some 125,000 workers in the Canadian automobile assembly and parts sector and some 600,000 to 700,000 other workers in a whole range of other sectors whose well-being depends upon the well-being and health of the Canadian automotive industry. We, they, and the communities in which they live, expected more from the Government, although it is not the first time we have been disappointed at the inaction of the Government, and I am sure it will not be the last.
After all, the Government had since last September to conclude new arrangements on quotas with the Japanese. Yet on the basis of pretty solid information, we find that meaningful discussions by our officials in Japan with Japanese authorities began only some 10 days ago. We now find that the deadline of March 31 is fast approaching, and the Government is saying nothing more than that the discussions are continuing.
The Minister has disappointed us in another important way. In his statement he said that the Government had reviewed its policy, but that is all he said. He did not take this opportunity to disclose to the House and to Canadians exactly what is and what will be its policy on the Canadian automotive industry, yet the industry is absolutely crucial to the well-being of the Canadian economy.
All or almost all of the increase in the Gross National Product in Canada last year came from the recovery of the Canadian auto industry. All or almost all of our record trade

March 29, 1985
Automobile Quotas
surplus last year came from the exports of the Canadian auto industry. This recovery came from a firm and definite public policy, put into place and successfully carried out by the previous Liberal Government. The previous Liberal Government was willing to step in, in support of business and labour in the automotive sector, to help that sector modernize, restructure and fight back against the onslaught of the world recession and competition from Japanese and other imported cars. It negotiated the arrangement with Chrysler which enabled that company to survive, to flourish and to save 10,000 jobs directly and triple that amount in supplier firms. It stepped in and worked out an arrangement with the Ford Motor Company which prevented its key plant in Oakville from closing and encouraged that company to remodel that plant to produce a new line of front-wheel drive cars.
It created the Industry and Labour Adjustment Program which provided Canadian parts manufacturers with the capital they needed to invest in the high-tech equipment, which was essential if these companies were to be able to compete for the parts business of North America. It also put in place the Industrial and Regional Development Program which succeeded ILAP. Before the Government changed it was responsible for levering, along with FIRA, some $2.5 billion in new automotive investment-for example, the American Motors project in Brampton, as well as the General Motors projects in Oshawa and St. Catharines.
All this was done in the context of the achievement of the previous Liberal Government in getting the Japanese to enter into quota arrangements-let us call them that, because that is what they are-to restrain the pace of exports of Japanese cars into the Canadian market. These arrangements gave the industry a needed breathing space to carry out the already highly successful task of restructuring and rebuilding.
Now, when the industry is saying very clearly that although it has made progress in that restructuring a further period of breathing space is required, the Government, despite all the time it had to do so, is saying only that it is continuing discussions with the Japanese.
Also, when the industry is saying to the Government that Canada needs the levers provided by the quota arrangements in order to get the Japanese to make commitments to put in Canada something they have not done already, that is, a fair share of their investment, production and jobs in the North American auto sector, all the Government can tell us is that it is continuing discussions.
What the Government should be doing privately, and more important publicly, is saying to the Japanese that the quotas we now have will remain unless and until they make meaningful and binding commitments to invest, to produce and to provide jobs in Canada equivalent proportionately to what they have already begun to do in the United States. Those quotas, the Government should be telling the Japanese, have to remain in place until the Japanese agree to accept the same rules as North American producers for production, investment and jobs in Canada as a condition of access to our market.
Why did the Minister not have the courage to rise and send that clear message in the forum of the House of Commons to the Japanese today? All he said was that the Minister for International Trade (Mr. Kelleher) was sending a letter to his Japanese counterpart. We need more than that. We need the Minister in Japan having some tough discussions with the Japanese to get the kinds of results about which I am talking for the Canadian auto worker and the Canadian economy in general.
I want to be fair about this. At least the Minister responded to one of my requests, and that was, to tell the Japanese that they would not be allowed to flood the Canadian market if no agreement was in place on March 31. The Minister's words were vague-and that is unlike him-and loose.

The Government has to tell the Japanese that what is going on in the United Sates does not provide a basis for arrangements between Japan and Canada on the sending of cars from their country to our country. The United States is the largest and most powerful economy in the world. It has an economic clout without quotas. To get the kind of commitments for investment in this country which we have just begun to get without the levers of quotas or measures like the IRDP and FIRA measures, which the Government is already, unfortunately, starting to weaken. The Americans seemed to have made an arrangement with the Japanese to allow a 24 per cent increase in exports from Japan to that country. We have to send the Japanese a clear message that that is not right, that that is not what should be done for Canada.
We have a very different position. As I said, we have to send a clear signal to the Japanese that the quotas at the present level have to remain until the kinds of arrangements sought by the auto task force, a unanimous consensual recommendation by the assemblers, parts manufacturers and the union, are put in place. If this is not by negotiation, then the Government has to be willing to proceed by legislation, if that alternative is necessary.
It appears what the Minister is doing is to facilitate the efforts by Mr. Miller of Ontario to get re-elected. We have to be afraid that there is bad news in store for the auto workers of Ontario. The Canadian Government wants that Ontario election out of the way. At the very least, the statement today is sending a message to Mr. Miller that he does not have the clout he is telling the people of Ontario he has with this Government.
In conclusion, this is a very disappointing statement from the Government. It told the Canadian people it would do more and produce better. It has not done so. It is a matter of
March 29, 1985

concern, and I say this on behalf of the Official Opposition, the auto workers and the Canadian economy, that so little has been done by a Government which claims it has the authority and the mandate to do more. It has let down the Canadian people once too often.

Second, we have also had the sense that these VER arrangements were absolutely crucial to push the Japanese to put into this country the kinds of levels of investment which Canada deserves. We heard from the Minister that something in the order of $100 million in investment has been made by Japanese car companies in this country compared to $5 billion in the United States. Therefore, these arrangements have been crucial. We must continue to enforce that kind of bargaining leverage that we need. It is important to note that public opinion polls which have been done in the last few weeks indicate that the great majority of Canadians support these quota arrangements. The Minister will appreciate that my figures are also very rough because I have not had a lot to go on. In 1980, the best year on
March 29, 1985

record that 1 have, the pre-tax income of the Bank was equivalent to .85 per cent of its assets. In 1981 it was .8 per cent. In 1982, it was .55 per cent. In 1983 it was .35 per cent. In 1984, the Bank actually had a pre-tax loss of $8 million, although that is carefully disguised from the shareholders in the annual report. Its loss was equivalent to a return on assets of minus .25 per cent. In 1985 the Bank can expect about $25 million in income if it lends the $250 million at 10 per cent for half the year, which is what it will have the money for effectively. That will give it an income of $12 million from the injection of funds. However, it is going to have a pre-tax profit of zero according to the Minister so it is going to lose $12 million on all the rest of its business, based on some $3 billion worth of assets, for a negative return on assets of .4 per cent.
The Minister says that the Bank will have a pre-tax income in 1986 of around $12.4 million, half of which will be available for repayment, according to the Bank's estimates. If the pre-tax income is $12 million, and if $25 million is earned on that $250 million which is coming from the support group, then the Bank's loss on its other business will be of the order of $12 million, for a negative return on assets of .35 per cent. In 1987 the Bank, according to her figures, will have a profit of about $32.8 million, but $25 million of that, if interest rates stay at present levels, would come from the injection from the support group. Therefore, the Bank's profit on its other business will be $7 million, approximately, or equivalent to .2 per cent on assets, bearing in mind that the assets are likely to grow because some of the retained profit will allow an increase in assets.
In 1988 there will be $34 million in pre-tax income, $25 million will come from the revenue earned on the interest free loans from the support group, and $9 million will be earned on some $4 billion worth of assets. That is equivalent to about .2 per cent. In 1989 I reckon that the return will be about $13 million apart from what is earned on the Government's $250 million, or .3 per cent.
These figures are open to correction but that is a pretty lousy outlook and this is an outstanding example of corporate welfare. We used to have corporate welfare from the Liberal Government of Canada, and now we have it from the Conservative Government. Of course, this does not factor in the specific and unusual risks, given the fact that more than one third of the Bank's assets are concentrated in a foreign jurisdiction, in California, which could be open to completely different circumstances than here in Canada.
