An all-Party consent shows there is obviously a need to carry out an investigation into the recent collapse and rescue of the Canadian Commercial Bank which is based in western Canada and now operates across the country. 1 believe that the time to carry out an investigation is before we agree to bail out the Bank. We felt that if we were going to do this, the least we could do is to call for a special investigation. We are pleased that that opportunity will follow, but it does seem to be putting the cart before the horse to pass this Bill in order to build confidence within the financial community. Sometime in the future we will find out what went wrong.
I appreciate the comments of the Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall) in response to our questions today, but they leave many unanswered questions. There are a variety of questions regarding the role of the Governor of the Bank of Canada in this process. There are questions about the ability of the Inspector General of Banks to carry out his responsibility of overseeing the banking community of Canada. It is questionable whether he has the appropriate authority and staff to do the job which is required during these difficult times. We have questions about the ability of a single individual, using shady and questionable means, to obtain a considerable portion of this particular Bank, which goes against the principle of the Bank Act limiting ownership by one individual or corporation to 10 per cent.
The Government's enthusiasm to bail out this or any particular bank is brought into question. The Bank itself has unquestionably foreclosed on all sorts of individuals, small businesses, ranchers, and farmers in western Canada. It has become traditional for banks across the country to act very callously in many cases. In order to look good on their quarterly reports and to enable their loans officers to have a good track record, they rip the rug out from under small businesses. They have little care for the small business community. When it comes time for the Government to respond to the banks, rather than the small businesses, farmers, ranchers, or
homeowners, it falls over itself with enthusiasm for bailing out this corporate institution.
Traditionally banking colleagues would have come together to bail out this Bank. However, in this case they knew they had a good partner. The banks contribute substantially to the political coffers of the Progressive Conservative Party and they knew they could count on the Government of Canada when it came to a crunch. While they as bankers would have to come up with a few hundred million dollars, they knew they had buddies in the Government of Alberta and the Government of Canada whom they could call upon to come up with an extra $75 million of the people of Canada. Taxpayers' dollars are being used to bail out the tenth largest Bank in Canada. That is the ultimate in corporate welfare.
If there is a set of financial institutions that do not require assistance from the taxpayers of Canada, it is certainly the banking community. After all, it is not uncommon at all to find return on equity of 15 per cent to 18 per cent during these very difficult times. If any sector of the economy can move in to save its brethren, it is certainly the banks. It is certainly disappointing that the Government has seen fit to ask the taxpayers of Canada, who are struggling simply to keep afloat, to use those dollars to bail out the Bank.

On two occasions in the last 15 years, when two regional banks were in difficulty, the banks themselves moved to provide solutions by mergers.
In this case there never would have been any question of liquidation. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to make a few comments regarding this legislation. It is interesting to note, from the remarks of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Crosbie) and other speakers, that the discussion has primarily centred on certain changes that will take place in April as certain aspects of the Charter come into force.
Bill C-27, an Act to amend certain Acts having regard to the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, will amend existing federal legislation to bring it in line with the Charter of Rights.
We have heard Canadians talk about the various sections of our society that they feel are being discriminated against by certain laws in this country, both federal and provincial. Today I would like to refer to certain discriminatory federal regulations that were introduced by the present Government. There are cases which have come to the attention of many people since last year. Let me cite a case that was referred to the Minister of Justice by the town council of Centreville. They objected to the fact that the Department of Manpower and Immigration was demanding that the town council repay funds to the Government because one of the council's employees should not have been hired by the town council. In fact, that particular employee was a student and the son of the town clerk of this particular council.
I have a copy of the letter that was written to the Minister of Justice. It says that the Town of Centreville sponsored a program employing six students. One week after the project commenced, the council was asked by an official from the Department to fire one of the students because he was the son of the town clerk. The letter went on to state that the fact that
Statute Law Amendment Act
the student's mother worked for the town council was, in the opinion of the council, insufficient reason to fire the student. Therefore he was employed for the duration of the project.
The council went on to make a very interesting statement. It said that the federal Government officials are trying to save a mere $1,110 on a technicality that is unfair and violates the human rights regulation that prohibits the council from asking any prospective employee questions regarding relatives.
The town council of Centreville has written to the Minister of Justice to ask for his intervention. The Minister of Justice has not intervened. The town council has been asked to pay this money to the federal Treasury at least 12 times since the letter was written to the Minister of Justice.
I have given this example because it raises some interesting questions. According to the human rights regulations, this town council is not allowed to ask about the family of a prospective employee. I took the liberty of writing to the Canadian Human Rights Commission because this same rule applies to every municipal body in Canada. Every municipal body that receives a student employment program is not allowed to hire a student who is the son or daughter of someone who signs the contract for the project.
There are provincial laws which say that in order for a municipality to sign a contract with the federal Government or other agency, any contract must be signed by the mayor or, deputy mayor and the town clerk. In the case of rural Newfoundland, the town clerk might be making $50 a week, that person might have nothing to do with the hiring of students, but because provincial regulations obligate that person to sign the contract, his or her son or daugher is not allowed to work on any federally funded project.
The importance of this question relates to hundreds of municipalities in Newfoundland alone and to every municipality in Canada.
I received a rather interesting response from the Canadian Human Rights Commission. It says that the Canadian Human Rights Act specifies that it is discriminatory for an employer to pursue a policy or practice which adversely differentiates on the basis of race, national or ethnic origin, colour, religion, age, sex, marital status, family status and so on.
The assertion by the town council was absolutely correct. It was not allowed to distinguish between the employees it was hiring and it was not allowed to discriminate on the basis of the family status of that particular student.
The Canadian Human Rights Commission goes on to point out that as far as this particular problem is concerned:
I have been informed that all programs administered by the Federal Government includes such a "Conflict of Interest" clause. The relevant policy comes from Terms and Conditions approved by the Treasury Board-
On the one hand, municipalities are not allowed to hire a family member of someone who signs a contract because of conflict of interest regulations. Yet the town council in this particular case is not allowed to question the family relations of the person whom they are hiring.

March 29, 1985

The legislation before us today contains no method for correcting that single aspect of the Student Employment Program or of any particular grant given by the federal Government to any agency or association in this country. The bottom line is that the town council of Centreville in this case is being hounded and told that it must pay the money back to the federal Government that was paid to this university student who came home for the summer and was hired and just happened to be the son of the town clerk in that community.
The Minister of Justice and the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) received a letter from that town council saying, "Will you please forgive this money because we cannot afford to pay it back". There was no answer. The only answer sent was from the Minister referring to conflict of interest guidelines. In other words, in that particular community there were two university students who came home for the summer. There were five jobs. People were told they were not allowed to hire one university student, that they must take the other university student plus four students from grade 12 or grade 11 because the mother of the student who came home for the summer was making $50 a week as the town clerk. The other university student was not allowed to be employed through that particular grant. Letters were written to two Cabinet ministers and the answer was, "No, you have to pay up from your municipal taxes".
This is a case of outright discrimination, Mr. Speaker. 1 cannot think of a more specific case of outright discrimination in a student employment program. It is outright and total discrimination.
To continue for a moment on that particular program, let me say that what you perceive in the House of Commons and what reports that are done for the Government of Canada show, with recommendations on how to do away with discrimination, is that sometimes when you get down to the grass roots those very reports and rules and regulations that are adapted and put into legislation are seen to discriminate against the ordinary person in the small rural areas. I give you as an example, Mr. Speaker, the regulations that were sent down last week by the Minister of Employment and Immigration to all the Manpower offices saying that the residency requirement for federal jobs must be removed. In other words, if you have a grant going into the community of Centreville or any other community across Canada this summer, then that grant could be used to fill jobs with students from St. John's, Newfoundland; Gander, Newfoundland; Corner Brook, or Quebec City, if the job suits somebody in Quebec City. Every Member of the House, except me, would say yes, that the residency requirement for federal jobs should be lifted, that you should be free to move within a system right across this country.
Just as you have a rule on conflict of regulations in effect, so you should not have the residency requirement lifted for grants to high unemployment areas. The reason is quite simple. The federal Government assigns student employment money
mainly on the basis of unemployment rates. To allow the total mobility of students in works programs could mean that students from high employment areas could be filling jobs in the high unemployment areas. The reason is that the first people who are normally hired are the university students, and post-secondary students, and only after that are the secondary students taken on. I just wanted to mention that as it will be seen as discrimination by the people who live in those small communities.
I point to another discriminatory clause in the Student Employment Program. It says here that only those students can be hired who wish to return to school on a full-time basis in the fall. It is funny, isn't it, that somebody who has to go back to university for only one term is not a full-time student for that next year, somebody who has to go back and pick up two courses instead of five is not a full-time student for that year? Therefore, by regulation no part-time students, no student going back for one period of the year, one semester, is allowed to be hired by a student employment project this summer, none. That is another example of what people would perceive to be discrimination.
When you look at the Bill that modifies federal laws you are looking at changes to laws that satisfy a particular philosophy that the Government comes up with as a result of reports and investigations and commissions appointed by the Government. When you look at the grass roots level, the discrimination remains and it even intensifies sometimes because you try to remove discrimination. That is the point. It is unfortunate that the Government of Canada cannot see that.
I will give you another reference, Mr. Speaker. This is a letter that was sent to a newspaper from the chairperson in a community called Too Good Arm. This letter was published in a newspaper two days ago. It reads;
Please allow me space in your paper to express my views on a Canada Works project in our community. Our committee applied for a grant in October, 1984-
It received a project. The letter goes on:
The next step was to wait for Manpower in Gander to refer names of people needing jobs. When they sent out the names we had 12 names including one man who's been in Alberta since September 1984. Our committee was not satisfied with these names. So we contacted Canada Manpower in Gander for more names. Our committee had a list of names taken from our community who wanted jobs, and who needed them badly, but Manpower refused to even discuss the list of names we had.
After fighting tooth and nail with Manpower they finally sent out another list of names. On this list was mostly fishermen and fish-plant workers. Why, we asked, did Manpower send out those names to us. Because these people had jobs waiting for them in April or May of 1985.
We, as a committee, were very disappointed because we had citizens from our community who needed this work. We had young people who needed it badly. We had workers, who worked on our Project in March of '84 and needed five more UlC weeks to qualify for UIC benefits, but Manpower would not refer their names so we could not hire them.
Our committee contacted the MHA from our area and we also had James Morgan working on this problem but no way would Manpower go along with any of us.
We would like to know why Manpower is so strict with our citizens who are not in the labour force.
March 29, 1985

It concludes:
When election time rolls around again let's just keep our votes or let's vote for Manpower in Gander because apparently they are the voice of our province.
It is signed by Madeline Hale, Chairperson for Local Improvement Committee, Too Good Arm. I have made reference to this before. There it is in black and white in a letter to the editor. The fact is that in all direct federal employment programs a person who has not drawn unemployment insurance is not allowed to be referred to a job. The fact is that a woman who has been out of the workforce for more than a year and a half is not allowed to be referred to a federal works program. The fact is that in order for a person to get a job he or she would have to be on unemployment insurance.
We are talking about high unemployment in rural areas across the country. What do people see? They see a student program for the summer to hire students with a built-in discrimination in it that I have already mentioned. They see a federal works program coming into their community with built-in discrimination in the program. Then they turn on their television sets and see the Minister of Justice introducing a Bill in the House of Commons to end discrimination in federal laws. They ask whether that means that young people are now allowed to go to work, that women are allowed to go to work or that people who have never been in the workforce will now be able to get referrals on federal works programs. No, it does not. That has not even been touched. In other words, the very things which matter are not even under discussion.
The Student Employment Program starts this summer, and the discrimination continues. If we looked at all the reports, studies and commissions, we would not even see the matter receiving a footnote reference. In the case to which 1 referred in the community of Centreville, the Minister of Justice should relent and get in touch with the Minister responsible to forgive that $1,110 bill of that student who found employment last summer. The same should be done for every student across the country who was penalized and discriminated against, as well as every student who will be discriminated against this summer.
The Minister of Employment and Immigration should take a look at her own programs and end the discrimination in them. She talks about ending discrimination against women and young people, yet they are the ones who are being discriminated against in her own programs. Even the Minister of Justice talks about curing the problem of discrimination. They may be curing the problem of discrimination in the eyes of people who do not really know what discrimination is. They may be doing that in some cases. They may be solving a national problem which should be solved, but they must take a second look to see what effect the removal of the residency requirement from jobs in Canada Manpower or what effect discrimination in the terms of reference or on priority lists for hiring on federal projects will have on small communities.
When the Minister of Justice returns from trying to get the Tories elected in Newfoundland, which he will not be able to

do, he should deal with the real problems facing people in high unemployment areas and end the real discrimination against the very poor caused by the Government of Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it gives me a great deal of pleasure to rise today to talk about Bill C-27 and about the very broad issue of equality rights. Throughout history, legislators, philosophers, judges, kings and queens have all wrestled with the concept of equality. Here in Canada, our jurists and politicians have debated the issue of equality for over 100 years. In 1960, the Government under Prime Minister John Diefenbaker took a major step in protecting basic human freedoms by introducing the Bill of Rights. For the first time in history, Canadians had a document which set out the fundamental rights and freedoms to which each and every person was entitled. Then in 1982 the Government introduced as part of the Constitution Act a Charter of Rights and Freedoms. My Party supported a fair, just and practical Charter. We spoke out for all Canadians and fought to ensure that the provinces were given their rightful place in the patriation process.
Today, three years following the passage of the Constitution, we move forward to April 17 when the equality provision, Section 15 of the Charter, comes into force. Section 15 of the Charter provides for equality before and under the law. It also provides for equal protection and equal benefit of the law without discrimination based upon race, origin, colour, religion, sex, age or mental or physical disability.
The challenge before us as Members of the House is to define exactly what equality means. How do we judge equality in our laws? What is a just or an unjust law? St. Thomas Aquinas defined an unjust law as a human law which is not rooted in eternal law and natural law. A just law, according to St. Thomas, was any law that uplifts human personality. Any law that degrades human personality is unjust.
Martin Luther King defined an unjust law as a code that a numerical or power majority group compels a minority group to obey but does not make binding on itself. A just law is a code that a majority compels a minority to follow and that the majority is willing to follow itself. It is this latter code of just law that our Government under the Charter of Rights must develop.
The challenge now before us in the House is to define equality and apply that definition to over 1,000 federal statutes. The process will not be easy. It will take a great deal of cautious and careful consideration. Bill C-27 marks the beginning of enacting Section 15 of the Charter of Rights.
Some specifics, as Section 15 relates to certain existing legislation, are addressed in Bill C-27. As I have listened to Hon. Members speak on the Bill, it has been my opinion that although they are in favour of it, they feel it does not go far enough. Section 15 of the Charter of Rights raises many basic and far-reaching questions. For example, should mandatory retirement be abolished? Do the Unemployment Insurance Act and federal pension laws discriminate unfairly against women? What laws should be changed to ensure equality for the

physically or mentally handicapped? These far-reaching questions, as well as many others, will be the subject of review by a parliamentary committee of the House. This committee will reach out to Canadians, will listen and will hear the views, ideas and suggestions of the people as they relate to these many issues.

speechtext:
Yes, my hon. friend is correct. The committee will travel from coast to coast to hear the views of all Canadians. It is my privilege to be one of the seven members of this committee. I am pleased to be one of the vice-chairpersons of it, sharing my position with the Hon. Member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Tremblay).
Section 15 will touch upon every aspect of Canadian life. Literally, millions of words clarifying, shaping, defining and moulding Section 15 to the realities of Canadian society can be expected in the months, years and decades ahead.
I want to mention briefly a few areas of particular concern to me and to the people of Scarborough Centre, the riding which I represent. I wish to speak of the equality provisions and our great multicultural heritage. Canada has been built by a unique blend of cultural identities. Our country takes pride in the cultural diversity and a multi-ethnic heritage. Thousands and thousands of people come to Canada every year because in Canada they can be free. Indeed, Canada is a nation of immigrants and we must ensure that cultural equality is protected and enhanced. As Section 27 of the Charter states, and I quote:
This Charter shall be interpreted in a manner consistent with the preservation and enhancement of the multicultural heritage of Canadians.
Our laws must protect this cultural diversity. Cultural equality means giving all Canadians, regardless of their race or ethnic background, an equal opportunity to live, to work and to prosper in this great nation of ours.
Let me turn to Bill C-27. There are three important issues addressed in Bill C-27. First, there is the elimination of in camera hearings as currently provided for under the Immigration Act. These are going to be eliminated, with the exception of those cases where undue publicity may be generated by an open hearing. This will ensure that immigration hearings will be open, in the public and fair.
Second, the Canadian Human Rights Commission will no longer have the power to select members of tribunals established to rule on discrimination cases under the Human Rights Act. Rather, tribunal members will be chosen by an independent official to be appointed by the Governor in Council. Third, persons 18 years of age will now be able to serve as corporation board members. This will bring some uniformity to the law which presently allows persons of 18 years of age to vote, but does not recognize his or her right to serve as a responsible member of a board of directors.
On the broader issues, a group of people in our society who will be anxiously awaiting the application of Section 15 is the disabled. Discrimination, especially in the job market, based on mental and physical disability must be eliminated. Canadians are becoming more and more aware of the important contribution disabled people are making to our society. Numerous equality questions relating to the disabled in relation to military service, immigration and unemployment insurance must be answered. Most recently, last week there was a demonstration held in relation to the opening of a new transit line in Scarborough. An outstanding activist for the disabled, Beryl Potter, led the demonstration at the opening of that transit line. She was demonstrating for access to public transportation in the Toronto Transit Commission. I applaud her for the actions she took.
There are many issues affecting the lives of millions of Canadians that are part of Section 15 of the Charter. A significant piece of legislation that will need review is the National Defence Act. A greater degree of equivalency between the code of service discipline and criminal law must be established. We must ensure that all legal rights and guarantees provided to citizens under the Criminal Code are applied equally to the members of the military.
A variety of equality issues relating to age and sex will also need careful examination as a result of Section 15. Is the calculation of pensions sexually biased? In addition, is it fair that home-makers in this country are denied the right to contribute to and benefit from the Canada Pension Plan? This is a national program in which a large number of Canadians are denied access to participate, although they maintain and foster the family values by caring for the children who will become the next generation of Canadians. This is an important issue that we will be discussing, and it is an issue on which we will be looking for action in the near future.
In addition, there are further issues that have been dealt with by other Ministries relating to this section of the Constitution. In particular, the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Crombie) recently brought forth legislation, part of which relates to the reinstatement of the status of Indian women who have married outside their culture. Having attended and participated in a number of the meetings of the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs, I understand the complexity of this issue and that it will take time to resolve. The legislation is courageous. It is the first step in correcting a serious injustice to Indian women.
Similarly, our Government has taken action in relation to the Abella report. Crown corporations must begin implementing employment equality by September and begin reporting annually within a year. Federally-regulated businesses with more than 100 employees must develop plans and begin reporting within three years. Companies tendering on government contracts for goods and services must certrify their commitment to employment equality and show results. These announcements were made recently by the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) on behalf of this Government. That Minister has been a strong champion
March 29, 1985

and a consistent voice for human rights and equality rights. She must be commended for her oustanding efforts and now for her actions. To ensure a broad range of discussions on issues, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Crosbie) has wisely set up a subcommittee of the Justice Committee to solicit the views of Canadians from coast to coast.
Following discussions with Canadians in the next few months, it is our duty as legislators to outline the policy options for just and fair laws. The ideas, direction and principles must come from the people, through the committee to this House. We cannot simply declare that Section 15 will now suddenly come into effect. Our Government believes in establishing the direction and the principles for Section 15 here in Parliament and with the Canadian people. That is the purpose of this committee. It will meet Canadians from all walks of life to discuss their views, their interpretations and their feelings on Section 15.
The work of the committee is crucial in establishing a format for the equality provisions. The people have a right to be heard on such an important matter and they will be heard by this Government. My Party believes that the principles of law must be established here in Parliament with input from the people and not in a courtroom by a judge. Canadians want Section 15 to apply in a practical and workable fashion. Canadians have entrusted to us the huge responsibility of ensuring that it applies justly and fairly to the Canadian way of life.
On April 17, Section 15 will become a vibrant and real part of our society. Let us hope that as long as Canada exists as a nation, the pursuit of equality and justice will be paramount in this House of Commons.

SUGGESTED NEW LEGISLATION Mr. Edouard Desrosiers (Hochelaga-Maisonneuve) moved:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of introducing legislation to:
(1)	dissolve the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and establish a new broadcasting corporation devoted to Canada's cultural development;
(2)	terminate the present mandate of all members of the Corporation's Board of Directors and its offices abroad, including the management of CBC International; and
(3)	provide for a mechanism for replacing the new corporation's management, including the ratification of their appointment by a Parliamentary committee.
He said: Mr. Speaker, only a few years ago, the Government was urging the CBC to "build the future", to pave the way to a distinct society, and it defined its philosophy as follows: to act now.
First, ensure that our broadcasting system supports our social and cultural orientations, recalling our commitment to the objectives defined in the Broadcasting Act in 1968.
Second, offer all Canadians a substantial number of attractive Canadian programs in all programming categories, while promoting the development of our broadcasting and visual production industries.
Third, to provide for diversified and expanded programming in both official languages and in all regions of Canada. The Government even suggested a thorough study. What has happened since then?
Mr. Speaker, using as an excuse the much needed budgetary cutbacks of $75 million, last November CBC administrators decided to create an uproar among the Canadian public. That is the way it is perceived by many Canadians. I have been receiving many letters and documents as well as telephone calls to this effect, and my colleagues as well. We have learned some troubling facts, and they should be taken seriously. We are a responsible Government that will not bow to threats or blackmail or let itself be influenced by undemocratic activities as low and unconscionable as those I am going to discuss with you now.
To raise a surge of protest among the Canadian public, the CBC has gone so far as to flout elementary decency and deprive Canadians in various regions across this country of a service to which they are entitled. Always claiming the pressure of budgetary restrictions instead of putting a stop to its own profligate spending, the CBC has cut what are commonly referred to as the antennae that relay programs from the stations to Canadian viewers and listeners. This is despicable, Mr. Speaker.
Under the same false pretences, the Corporation has cut popular programs to shock and win over public opinion. It asks the average employee to resign so that it can maintain the jobs

of friends who have long outlived their usefulness and to maintain jobs that themselves have become useless.
During this period of austerity, at a time when it is supposedly lacking in funds, the CBC is still publishing a kind of weekly that is sent from coast to coast across this country. In addition, just when the Government wants the CBC to cut expenditures, the corporation buys full-page ads in newspapers throughout Canada. How much does that cost, Mr. Speaker? No wonder people are asking questions.
Here is another example of outright waste of money, Mr. Speaker. Recently the management of engineering on Montreal's Cote de Liesse practically turned the place upside down-nothing new for them, but quite unacceptable to us. More than half of the 300 employees were moved from the second to the third floor, and vice versa. Some of those people have been uprooted anywhere from seven to twenty times over the years. How much does all that cost, year in and year out? The question is relevant indeed. So they were given seven francophone assistants to answer the phone.

Did you know that the production and support crew are forced to stay at the hotel of friends? Mr. Speaker, I want to dissociate myself completely, both personally and as a Member of the New Democratic Party, from the comments that were just made by the Hon. Member for Hochelaga-Maisonneuve. [English]
I want to say a few words in English because there may well be Canadians watching the parliamentary television channel right now who are wondering what this debate is about, particularly when we reflect upon the fact that it is a CBC channel which is carrying the record of the House of Commons debates into Canadian homes.
The proposal by the Hon. Member for Hochelaga-Maisonneuve (Mr. Desrosiers) is to dissolve the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and establish a new broadcasting corporation devoted to Canada's cultural development. He wishes to terminate the present mandate of all members of the Corporation's Board of Directors and its offices abroad, including the management of CBC International, and he wants a mechanism for replacing the new corporation's management, including the ratification of their appointment by a parliamentary committee. Let me deal with these points in reverse order.
During the election campaign, the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) promised that there would be a means by which all appointments could be ratified or at least considered by parliamentary committees. Nothing has been done about that in the last eight months. Yet the Member for Hochelaga-Maisonneuve seems to indicate that we should focus on CBC-Radio Canada. I suggest it concerns a broader question to which we should have had answers by now. 1 urge the Hon. Member to consult with his Prime Minister and suggest some action.
I believe there can be only one purpose behind the idea to terminate the present mandate of all members of the Corporation's Board of Directors. The Conservative Party wants to take similar action with the CBC-Radio Canada as it did with Air Canada and VIA Rail. In other words, the Conservatives want to appoint Conservatives with a good record of service to
March 29, 1985

the Party and put that above the service of the Board of Directors of CBC-Radio Canada to the people of Canada.
More important, if I understood the Hon. Member correctly, he is suggesting that all offices of the CBC abroad should be closed. He mentioned cities like London, Washington and Moscow. I presume that he believes that our news service abroad through the CBC should be shut down. That is the major activity in those offices abroad.
Perhaps he thinks we should no longer be trying to sell award winning programs like the Nature of Things around the world through the facilities of CBC offices abroad. He must believe that we should not seek to protect those kinds of images of Canada in other parts of the world.
The Hon. Member suggests that the management of CBC International should be shut down. I do not know if he wishes to terminate CBC International, but it broadcasts now in 12 different languages to Africa, Latin American and Europe. It is a major means of communicating what is happening in Canada. In fact, my hon. friends who have travelled to the United States will know that certain programs such as As it Happens from CBC Radio are regularly broadcast on public radio networks in the United States and are a very good voice for Canadians visiting our neighbours to the South.
The Hon. Member suggests that we should dissolve the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and establish a new broadcasting corporation devoted to Canada's cultural development. The mandate of the CBC is Canadian cultural development.

What I am afraid of particularly is that the comments of the Hon. Member for Hochelaga-Maisonneuve will affect the future of the CBC. Even if we do have a problem with American penetration on television channels, even in English Canada in Ontario, in the Western provinces and of course in Quebec, the vehicle of French culture, of Canadian culture in French in Canada is Radio-Canada, and I fail to understand why the Hon. Member wants to get rid of all Radio-Canada services and all the executives and terminate the contracts of all the performers and producers and all those people who work on Radio-Canada's news programs in the hope that we might be able to improve services.
Mr. Speaker, I think such comments do a disservice to the people of Quebec who have been very well served by Radio-Canada.

I am suggesting that it is particularly irresponsible to say that Radio Canada, the French language service of the CBC, should be terminated. The Hon. Member should know that Montreal is the first or second largest production centre of French language programming anywhere in the world and that it rivals the one in Paris, France. Certainly in quality we can easily stand up to Radio Television Frangais. This has been accomplished by Quebeckers, Canadiens Frangais, and I find
Broadcasting
it totally irresponsible that the Hon. Member, who represents les Quebecois, should make that suggestion.
I think it is totally irresponsible to suggest that the CBC English services should be disbanded and thrown to the six winds, as the Hon. Member suggests.
He is confusing a need which may exist for some cleaning out of the administration of the CBC on Bronson Avenue in the heart of Ottawa, with what happens in terms of programming. The Hon. Member may recall the report which came out on the CBC in 1960s, which said that the most important thing about the CBC is its programming, and everything else is housekeeping.
The institution has been with us for 50 years. There may be some need to improve the housekeeping. I have had some concerns that perhaps the cuts that have been imposed on the CBC by the Government have borne more on the programming content than on the administration, which does not actually deliver the programs. That is a specific problem on which I would not mind seeing some action. However, you do not throw the baby out with the bath water. You do not disband the CBC in order to reform it. It would be total wishful thinking to believe that we could, by terminating the CBC, establish and improve the service that would automatically enhance Canada's cultural development.
We must recognize that the problems facing the CBC now in terms of being an authentic voice for Canadian cultural development are related to the policies of the former Liberal Government, which are being continued by the new Government in terms of the misunderstanding of the mandate under the Broadcasting Act to use broadcasting in Canada as an instrument of Canadian cultural development.
The fact is that although that was the proposal in the Broadcasting Act, it has been substantially ignored. The situation has gone from bad to worse.
In the 1950s, the CBC was the vehicle of Canada's cultural expression, at least in television, because it was the only television in the country. With the creation of private broadcasting through the CTV, the CBC became responsible for half of the television broadcasting in this country. As a result of technological change which has permitted cable access to communities like Edmonton and Chicoutimi in the north, we have a situation where three-quarters of the television broadcasting in this country is not native broadcasting but comes from the United States.
In Europe they speak of the Canadianization problem. We think Canadianization is good, but in other countries Canadianization means the takeover of a country's broadcasting service by another country. Canada is the only major country in the world which allows its television broadcasting to contain the complete program output of another country. In our case it is the United States.
It is a fact that due to the neglect of the former Government and the present Government, a tremendous volume of television programming does not come from Canadian sources but from American sources. We must be aware of that situation

March 29, 1985
Broadcasting
and seriously address it. In considering this problem, let us not undermine and disband the major vehicle by which we identify and show Canadian cultural identity, the CBC and Radio Canada.
Let me comment on some of the points made in the Hon. Member's motion. The McKinsey review of the CBC indicated quite clearly that in operating in two official languages and covering a widely dispersed geography of 4,000 miles, the CBC faces more difficult and cost broadcasting challenges than do other public broadcasters. Notwithstanding that, the Corporation is substantially more efficient than other public broadcasters, measured by hours of programming output per employee and per dollar expenditures.
The major conclusion of the Auditor General's report a year or so ago was that the CBC needed long-term planning, but the CBC cannot do long-term planning unless it is assured of long-term dollars from the Government and neither the present nor the former Governments were prepared to make that particular commitment.
The McKinsey report said that, in comparison with the private sector:
-replacing the CBC with the private sector with its current economic structure would cost Canadians substantially more on a annual basis.
The CBC, despite some problems in delivering programs which may well exist, nonetheless, if you look at the over-all record, is quite extraordinary. The CBC produces twice as many hours of television programming per employee as other public networks. In prime time, Canadian content of the CBC runs 20 per cent to 40 per cent higher than CTV or Global. The CBC, which the Hon. Member wishes to disband, provides more prime time hours of Canadian content than both the CTV and Global combined.

In prime time, less than 25 per cent of programming on television is Canadian. Of that, three-fifths comes from the CBC. Only 5 per cent of TV drama that we see on our air
waves here in Canada is Canadian, most of it comes from the United States. I am talking about situation comedies such as "Dallas".
It is a deplorable fact that we are out-gunned 20 to 1 in terms of what appears on our air waves when it comes to drama. But 90 per cent of the t.v. drama which comes from Canadian sources is in fact Canadian. My hon. friend, the Member for Hochelaga-Maisonneuve, is suggesting that we disband the CBC in order to have more sitcoms that come from Hollywood and from New York and Chicago. That would appear to be the case he is making, Mr. Speaker. I would suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that the CBC is the only broadcasting company that has made a serious attempt to meet the Broadcasting Act, which calls for a broadcasting system that is predominantly Canadian.
If you want to speak about a Canadian cultural identity, "The National" on CBC reaches 5 million Canadians a week. Those are adult English-speaking Canadians. You are talking about 5 million Canadians a week out of a total audience in English Canada of perhaps 11 or 12 million adults. "The Journal" reaches 4 million Canadians a week. "The Fifth Estate", which is shown once a week, reaches 1.5 million Canadians a week. "Fraggle Rock" reaches 1.5 million children a week. "Tommy Hunter" gets 1.5 million people a week. "The Beachcombers" gets 1.25 million a week, a program that has entertained Canadians for years.

subtopic: CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION
speechtext: What about "The Friendly Giant"?

subtopic: CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION
speechtext:
I would like to see "The Friendly Giant" there. "Hockey Night in Canada" brings in between 2 and 3 million Canadians.
When a program like "Chautauqua Girl" on CBC, rivalled by programs in the United States which are extraordinarily well financed, gets 2.6 million people, blowing "The A-Team" and stuff like that right out of the water, when "The Grey Fox", a Canadian film on the CBC, drew 2.1 million people, and "Hockey Night", the drama about a girl who was kicked off a boys' hockey team, drew 2.2 million viewers, let us stop short-changing what we Canadians can do and are doing through the CBC.
I would like to point out to my hon. friend that what we are getting for that $800 million we spend on CBC amounts to 10c. a day for my family. Actually I think it is a little bit less than that, about 8 or 9c. a day. The English t.v. network cost only $200 million. It is not that expensive. We get 4,700 hours of programming, of which 2,000 hours is produced by the CBC. The AM radio network gives 5,000 hours, the stereo network 6,000 hours-

The CBC French television network, which is costing us $138 million every year, has 6,000 hours of programming, including 3,500 hours produced by the CBC. That, Mr. Speaker, exceeds the quality and quantity of French TV programs in Paris. On French radio, the 6,500 hours of AM programs cost
March 29, 1985

only $26 million a year, and on the French stereo network, only $8 million a year are spent for 7,000 hours of programs, including 6,000 hours produced by the CBC.
In addition, Mr. Speaker, we have 22,000 hours of programming, half of them from the CBC directly or regional TV stations, the CBC's 18 English regional TV stations, and 2,500 hours of programming on the CBC French regional TV station.
I could continue my remarks, Mr. Speaker, but all that goes to show that we do have a very important institution which is part of our existence.

To conclude, Mr. Speaker, if I can Find the quote, I would like to read a comment from David Suzuki, an eminent Canadian scientist and an eminent Canadian broadcaster. Mr. Suzuki has this to say:
The CBC has been a mirror for us to see ourselves as a people, the scope of this land, the challenge and our problems. Without the CBC, we would be a very different people and the poorer for it. Today, when we seem hell-bent on a path to greater integration into a North American context, 1 can't think of anything more important than the CBC for preserving that sense of difference that keeps many of us in this country. But now the CBC is in danger from a poorly thought-out attack.
I would say to my hon. friend from Hochelaga-Maisonneuve that really this is a poorly thought-out attack. He endangers Radio-Canada, and the CBC, the English-speaking network. He should realize that that has been one of the vital links, along with institutions like the Canadian National, the Canadian Pacific Railway, and Air Canada, which have helped bind this country together despite all the very strong influences from our North-South relationships with our friends to the South in the United States. The existence of the CBC for more than half a century has been one of the things that has enabled our country to maintain an independent sense of itself and has kept us from being swallowed up into the United States-

subtopic: CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION
speechtext: That is south of the border.

subtopic: CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION
speechtext:
Well, Mr. Speaker, it may be rather difficult from time to time for my friends in Quebec to understand. We, English Canadians, feel especially threatened by the cultural expansion of our American friends from south of the border. Quebec can safeguard its culture thanks to Radio-Canada for instance, and also to the fact that Quebec being a French community on an English-speaking continent, the cultural and language barriers make it easier for Quebecers to maintain their own culture. But for us in English Canada, this is a very serious and difficult task. We see in the CBC one of the strongest supports for Canadian culture and identity in English Canada.

It is for all these reasons, Mr. Speaker, that my Party and I entirely dissociate ourselves from this irresponsible and badly thought through resolution coming from the Hon. Member for
Broadcasting
Hochelaga-Maisonneuve. We ask him to reconsider and to work with us in order to ensure that in future the CBC can do a more effective job in terms, as he put it in his resolution, of ensuring Canada's cultural development and the maintenance of our identity as a nation.

speakeroldname: Mr. Geoff Scott (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Communications):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
subtopic: CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I consider it a privilege to address the motion before the House presented by the Hon. Member for Hochelaga-Maisonneuve (Mr. Desrosiers). I may have only a few moments before the Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod from the other place raps on the door. I am sure the Hon. Member would understand that if his motion passed, the lights would go out in this place and the CBC parliamentary service would be discontinued. However, on behalf of the Minister of Communications (Mr. Masse). I want to say that we respect some of the viewpoints of the Hon. Member for Hochelaga-Maisonneuve. He is a distinguished former President of the Union des Artistes in Quebec. He has reason to have very strong views about the Corporation, particularly about Radio Canada. However, I do not think it will come as any staggering surprise to him that the Minister of Communications and I will be arguing against his motion.
A few moments ago my colleague pointed out to the House that the Government had no control over CBC management under current legislation. We have no control precisely because it would hinder the Corporation from making truly independent program and journalistic decisions. He also referred to the importance of preserving the creative autonomy of the CBC. I should like to expand on this, if I may, for there is an implicit danger as I see it, particularly in the third part of his motion, which I feel should be articulated more explicitly.
The third part of the motion proposes the establishment of an appointment procedure for CBC management as distinct from its Board of Directors. The danger of interference in the CBC's day-to-day operations and administration, and especially in its programming matters, is something which concerns me and many of my colleagues, particularly those MPs like myself and like the NDP Member who spoke before me, who were trained in journalism.
Under current legislation, the Broadcasting Act, the executive vice-president is the only member of CBC management whose appointment is subject to ratification. The President of the Corporation recommends the appointee to the Board of Directors, and the Minister of Communications, in turn, recommends approval of the Corporation's appointment to the Governor in Council. In essence, the Corporation is the sole active agent in the appointment of its executive vice-president.
The Minister's recommendation to the Governor in Council acts as an indirect measure of accountability to the people of Canada. It is further desirable that Board of Directors appointments also involve some mechanism of accountability such as that described earlier by my colleague. However, senior management undertakes day-to-day operations and internal administration of the Corporation with the executive

March 29, 1985
Broadcasting
vice-president acting as the overseer. Especially with regard to program decision making, there should be no more involvement by government or Parliament. The CBC is free to appoint its senior management, and presumably selections are based upon the qualifications which perspective appointees have to offer to the competent administration of the Corporation and the Corporation's response to the needs of its audience.
I fear that if a parliamentary committee ratified CBC management appointments, the ability of the Corporation's management team to respond to the needs of Canadians, to respond effectively and decisively to the constantly changing Canadian broadcasting environment and to make competent, objective, independent decisions would be severely curtailed. How could a manager manage effectively when he or she is constantly looking over his or her shoulder? This is the kind of corporate planning that the third part of this motion could instil.
Recently the Minister of Communications reiterated the Government's commitment to public broadcasting, saying that the commitment was unswerving and fundamental. I should like to quote him. He said:
There are some principles which are clear now, and which will remain unchanged . .. (These include) our commitment to the need for a national public broadcaster, to the service to the country that such a broadcaster must provide, and our commitment to this country itself... (Canada is) a nation of diversity, of differing goals and ambitions and methods . . . But above all, a nation of talent and expression and dynamism ... a nation of greatness, which not only needs, but deserves, a public broadcaster equal to this greatness.
I simply do not see a CBC which would be equal to the greatness of Canada if it is forced to function in the kind of corporate environment this motion could create. This motion would contradict the Government's stated commitment to public broadcasting if it were allowed to pass, and programming would suffer.
Management is ultimately responsible for what we see and hear on the CBC. If CBC senior management appointees were to be ratified by a parliamentary committee as this motion proposes, there looms the potential for political or governmental interference in what we see and hear on the public network. I, for one, would find it difficult to trust the validity of news and information programming particularly. As a broadcast journalist by profession, I would be the first to jump up and down in protesting any involvement by Big Brother government in what we see and hear on the CBC. Simply knowing that the vice-president of news was appointed by a political process rather than by the Corporation itself would leave me to question everything I saw on "The National" or hear on "The World at Six". I wonder what viewers and listeners would think when the CBC reports on the parliamentary committee which would be responsible for ratifying the appointment of the manager who is ultimately responsible for the newscast in the first place.
This is not paranoia. This is fanciful hypothesizing. The motion would connect the CBC's programming, including news, to the political process. As has been argued countless times before, this is a dangerous connection to make. I can
quarrel and have quarrelled, as have many of my colleagues, with the CBC's treatment of news stories and its occasional bias in one particular political direction, but the Corporation has the right to determine its own programming. Even if there were no actual influence, the conenction to the political process would still exist and would make the CBC be seen by the public to be influenced by political pressures. That perception alone would be enough to undermine the trust which Canadians put in the CBC's information programming.
That is what is really at issue here. How would the CBC be perceived by its audience? This is a significant issue in the consideration of the motion before us which so far has gone neglected. If I may, I should like to discuss this in the remaining few moments.
As I mentioned, I have no doubt that some Canadians disagree from time to time with information which is broadcast by the CBC or dislike the way it is presented. With respect to entertainment programming, well, we are all critics, aren't we? Certainly the CBC broadcasts programs which some Canadians do not like. There is no way it could possibly please everybody all the time when it is in the business of entertaining. No medium can.
To be sure, none of the media is perfect, not even the television stations for which I used to work in the parliamentary Press Gallery. However, they serve an important social function as purveyors of information. The CBC's function is perhaps the most important of all Canadian media, given its audience reach and its excellent reputation in news and public affairs programming. The CBC, like the private networks, like the newspapers and like the weekly magazines, does not always tell us what we want to hear, but we need to hear it all the same. Perhaps the CBC does not always inform us as completely or as accurately as we would prefer, or as completely and as accurately as more ideal news-gathering conditions might permit. However, the CBC, and indeed all the media, strive to be as objective, accurate, fair and professional as possible. In the case of the broadcast media, licensees can be called to account for their programming when they appear before the Canadian Radio-Television and Telecommunications Commission for licence renewal. The public has a certain amount of trust in the media as sources of information, particularly in television, as studies have shown. Given the CBC's reputation for excellence, 1 would not be surprised if Canadians trust its news and information programming the most.
This motion would cause an element of doubt to be introduced into the relationship between the CBC and its audience. This could be considered as preventing the CBC from fulfilling its mandate.
